detailed_rationale:
SJVN Ltd (formerly Satluj Jal Vidyut Nigam) is a Navaratna-status (since Aug 2024) hydropower PSU generator, operating 1,972 MW of hydro capacity with a further 1,558 MW under construction, and diversifying into other renewables. FY26 revenue grew a strong 47% to Rs 4,528cr from Rs 3,072cr, but net profit actually fell 22% to Rs 642cr from Rs 818cr - a clear divergence between top-line growth and bottom-line delivery. This is exactly the kind of pattern we flag rather than credit: the revenue surge looks driven by new capacity coming online (and/or trading revenue) rather than by improving unit economics, and margins compressed from roughly 27% to 14% in the process.

The balance sheet shows why: SJVN is mid-way through a large, debt-funded capacity build-out (capital work-in-progress of roughly Rs 19,143cr), with free cash flow deeply negative (around Rs -3,839cr in FY26) as the company spends ahead of revenue. Return on capital employed has fallen from around 18% a decade ago to just 5.6% today, reflecting the low-return, long-gestation nature of new hydro capacity while it is under construction and not yet fully monetised. Debtor days are also elevated (162 days), consistent with the well-known sector-wide issue of state discoms delaying payments to generators.

We do not doubt the eventual value of a fully-commissioned 1,558 MW incremental hydro pipeline, but at a P/E near 43x for a business currently earning sub-cost-of-capital returns on a rapidly growing capital base, we think the market is paying up for future capacity before it has proven it can earn an adequate return once commissioned.
recommendation_rationale: The eye-catching 47% revenue growth is not backed by profit growth - it came with a 22% profit decline and material margin compression, which is a genuine earnings-quality flag, not a quality signal. Combined with declining ROCE and deeply negative free cash flow during a large capex cycle, we see this as a Sell rather than a rescue candidate.
summary: SJVN is a government-owned hydropower generator in the middle of a large capacity expansion, and while revenue grew sharply this year, profit actually declined as margins compressed - a sign that the new capacity has not yet translated into proportionate returns. Returns on capital have been falling for years as the company spends heavily ahead of revenue, and cash flow is currently negative. We would wait for the expansion to season and returns to recover before considering this name.
positive_para: Navaratna PSU status and a large, well-funded hydro and renewables capacity pipeline (1,558 MW under construction) provide genuine long-term growth optionality; government ownership provides funding access and policy support for the renewable transition.
negative_para: Profit fell 22% even as revenue grew 47%, showing the new capacity is not yet earning proportionate returns; ROCE has fallen from around 18% a decade ago to 5.6% today; free cash flow is deeply negative during the current capex cycle; and elevated debtor days reflect the sector-wide risk of delayed payments from state power distribution companies.
reverse_dcf_judgment: A ~43x P/E for a generator currently earning ROCE well below its cost of capital requires the market to be pricing multi-year-forward returns from capacity that has not yet been commissioned or seasoned - we would want to see ROCE stabilise and turn upward, and free cash flow turn less negative, before crediting that story.
